statement: This poster for Crunchies cereal shows a cartoon lion at a breakfast table. He is eating a big bowl of cereal and smiling. The kitchen is bright yellow and orange. The slogan says, "Roar into your day!" The cereal box is right next to him.

This billboard for Zippy lemonade shows a close-up of a tall glass of lemonade. It is full of ice, with a slice of lemon on top. Behind the glass, there is a hot, sunny beach with blue sea. The slogan says, "Cool down with Zippy."

In this TV commercial for Bubbles toothpaste, a boy brushes his teeth in a white bathroom. Then he smiles at the camera, and his teeth are very white. A short, happy song plays: "Bubbles, Bubbles, clean and bright!" The tube appears right at the end.

This flyer for Pizza Palace has a big photo of a hot pizza with cheese and tomatoes. At the top, red letters say, "Two for one on Tuesdays!" One large pizza costs £9. The phone number and address are at the bottom of the flyer.

In the window of Mila's Shoes, a long, bright red banner says SALE in big white letters. Under it, there are rows of shoes and boots. Small signs next to each pair say "Half price". The shop's name is in black letters above the door.

This poster for Sparkle shampoo shows a famous singer. There is a close-up of her face and her long, shiny hair. She is smiling and holding a pink bottle of shampoo. The brand name, Sparkle, is in silver letters at the top of the poster.

This carton of Moo Moo milk has a cartoon cow on the front. The cow is smiling and standing in green fields under a blue sky. A label on the side says "Fresh from the farm". The brand name is in big, round blue letters.

This pop-up appears on a phone screen while a teenage girl is reading. It is for a new game called GameZone. The word FREE flashes in huge yellow letters. There is a picture of a cartoon racing car, and a green button says "Play now".

In a supermarket, a woman stands at a table with a Choco Bite sign. She smiles and gives shoppers free pieces of a new chocolate bar. Behind her, there is a big poster with the brand's purple logo and a photo of the new bar.

This poster for Big Red Bus Tours shows a red bus in front of a famous clock tower in London. The sky is blue and the sun is shining. The headline says, "See London in one day!" Happy tourists wave from the open top deck.

In this TV commercial, a very dirty car drives into Speedy Car Wash. Water and soap go everywhere. A few seconds later, the car comes out clean and shiny. A catchy song plays: "Speedy, Speedy, wash it clean!" The slogan is "Shiny in five minutes."

This billboard for Panda Noodles shows a cartoon panda holding red chopsticks. In front of the panda, there is a close-up of a hot bowl of noodles with steam coming out. The panda looks happy and very hungry. The slogan says, "Noodles for every panda."

This poster for Sunny Farm eggs shows a farmer in a green field in the morning sun. She is smiling and holding a basket of fresh brown eggs. Chickens are walking around her feet. A label on the egg box below her says "Free range".

This flyer for City Gym shows a photo of people lifting weights. They look strong and happy. At the top, the headline says, "First month free!" Below the photo, it says the price after that is £20 a month. The address is at the bottom.

On the side of a city bus, there is a giant photo of one sandwich. It is full of chicken, cheese and lettuce, and it goes along the side of the bus. The brand name, Fresh & Go, is in green letters at the back.

This poster for Snowy ice cream shows a girl eating a big strawberry ice cream. She is sitting in a park on a hot summer day, and the sky is bright blue. The slogan says, "Cold, creamy, Snowy." The brand's logo is a white snowflake.

In this TV commercial for Happy Paws dog food, a brown dog hears a sound. It runs across the kitchen to its bowl. Then there is a close-up of the food. A short song plays, and the logo, a paw print, appears at the end.

In the window of TeaTime, there is a big photo of three tall cups of cold bubble tea. They are orange, pink and green. The headline says, "New flavour: mango!" A small sign next to the photo says that each large drink costs only ¥15.

This banner is at the top of a website called BookNook. It shows a row of colourful book covers: red, blue, yellow and green. Big black letters say, "Books from £2!" On the right-hand side, there is a bright orange button that says "Shop now".

This bag of Rocket crisps is shiny and orange. On the front, there is a cartoon rocket flying through space, with bright stars all around it. The brand name, Rocket, is in big, shiny silver letters. The bag also says "Cheese flavour" in small letters.

This poster for Star Cinema shows a close-up of a big box of popcorn. The popcorn is falling out of the box. The headline says, "Children go free on Sundays!" Under the headline, there are small pictures from three new films for all the family.

This billboard for Fizz energy drink shows a famous young footballer. He is standing on a football pitch and drinking from a cold blue can of Fizz. The Fizz logo, a yellow lightning bolt, is on the can. The slogan says, "Fizz. Feel the power."

This flyer for Clean Team shows a photo of a shining white kitchen. Everything is clean and tidy. The headline says, "We clean, you relax!" The price is £15 an hour. The phone number is in big blue letters at the bottom of the flyer.

This poster for Wonder Water Park shows three children coming down a long, twisting water slide. They are all laughing, and water is splashing everywhere. The colours in the poster are bright blue, yellow and red. The headline says, "Summer fun for all the family!"

In this TV commercial for Softy tissues, a little grey kitten is sleeping on a big pile of white tissues. The camera shows a close-up of its soft face. The colours are pale pink and white. A slow, quiet song plays: "So soft, so Softy."

This jar of Golden Honey has a drawing of a happy bee on the label. The bee is yellow and black, and it is flying over a pink flower. Under the bee, the label says "100% natural". The brand's logo is a small golden sun.

This poster for Speedy Bikes shows a girl riding a red bike down a green hill. She is smiling, and her hair is flying in the wind. The sky is bright blue. The slogan says, "Go further with Speedy." The logo is a red wheel.

This pop-up appears on a shopping website. It is for Fashion Fox, a clothes shop. Yellow letters on a black background say, "50% off all jeans today!" There is a photo of a pair of dark blue jeans and a button that says "Buy now".

This billboard for Mango Mobile shows a giant close-up of a new phone. The phone is gold and very thin and shiny. Above it, there is one word in big white letters: "Wow." The Mango Mobile logo, a small orange mango, is in the corner.

In the window of Toy Town, a person in a big brown teddy bear costume waves at the children. Behind the bear, there are shelves of toys. A big sign says, "Sale: all toys £5." The shop's name is in rainbow letters above the window.

This poster for Sleepwell beds shows a man asleep in a big, soft white bed. He is smiling. Through the window, there is a dark blue sky with lots of stars. The slogan says, "Sleep well, every night." The brand's logo is a silver moon.

In this TV commercial for Crispy Chick, a family sit at a kitchen table and eat fried chicken together. They are all laughing and talking. A catchy song plays: "Crispy, crunchy, Crispy Chick!" At the end, the red and yellow logo appears on the screen.

This flyer for the Lucky Dragon restaurant is red and gold. There is a picture of a gold dragon at the top. The headline says, "Chinese New Year special menu!" A meal for two costs ¥188. Photos of dumplings and fish are at the bottom.

This pot of Berry Blast yoghurt has big, bright red strawberries on the front. One strawberry is cut in half, and you can see it close up. The yoghurt inside is pink. The brand name is in big white letters on a dark purple stripe.

This poster for Greenhill Zoo shows a close-up of a baby elephant. It is standing next to its mother in a grassy park. The headline says, "Come and meet Lulu!" At the bottom, small letters say that the zoo opens every day at nine o'clock.

This billboard for Cool Breeze air conditioners shows a happy family relaxing in their living room. The room is light blue and white, and everyone looks calm. Outside the window, the sun is big, hot and orange. The slogan says, "Stay cool with Cool Breeze."

In the window of Petal, a flower shop, there are flowers in every colour: red, pink, yellow and purple. A big sign above them says, "Mother's Day is on Sunday!" Small white cards show the price of each bunch. A bunch of roses costs £20.

In this TV commercial for Quick Clean, a boy drops chocolate on his white T-shirt. His dad puts it in the washing machine. Then there is a close-up of the T-shirt, and it is white again. A short, happy song plays: "Quick Clean, Quick Clean!"

This poster for Rainbow paints shows a little girl painting a rainbow on her bedroom wall. She has paint on her hands and face, and she is laughing. The colours are very bright. The slogan says, "Paint your world." Paint tins stand next to her.

This flyer for Sun Travel has a photo of a beach with soft white sand and clear blue sea. There are palm trees and a small hotel. The headline says, "Holidays from £299!" The phone number and website are at the bottom of the flyer.

This billboard for Bolt e-scooters shows a woman riding a green scooter in the city. Next to her, there is a long line of cars that are not moving. She is smiling. The slogan says, "Beat the traffic." The Bolt logo is a lightning bolt.

This box of Little Bear biscuits is bright yellow. On the front, there is a photo of small biscuits in the shape of bears. A cartoon bear is holding one biscuit and smiling. The brand name is in big, round brown letters at the top.

This pop-up appears on a phone while a boy is watching a video. It is for the MusicBox app. There is a picture of a pair of black headphones. The headline says, "Free for three months!" A green button under the headline says "Start now".

This poster for Super Socks shows a famous basketball player. He is jumping high to the basket, and he is wearing bright green socks. The whole background is dark grey, so the socks are easy to see. The slogan, in white letters, says, "Jump higher."

In this TV commercial for Joy chewing gum, four young friends sit on the grass in a park. They laugh and blow big, round pink bubbles. A catchy song plays: "Chew, chew, chew some Joy!" At the end, the brand name appears in pink letters.

In the window of Coffee Corner, a big chalkboard says, "Free cookie with every coffee!" There is a drawing of a coffee cup and a cookie. Through the window, people are sitting at small tables and chatting. The café's name is painted on the glass.

This poster for the Night Fair shows a big wheel at night. It is covered in lots of bright lights: pink, blue and yellow. Families are walking around below it, eating candyfloss and laughing. At the top, the headline says, "Open every night in August!"

This bottle of Spring Peak water has a picture of tall, snowy mountains on the label. The sky behind them is light blue and clear. Under the mountains, the label says "Pure mountain water". The brand name is in dark blue letters above the picture.

This billboard for Tasty Burger shows a giant close-up of a burger. It has melted cheese, red tomato and fresh green lettuce. Right next to the burger, big, bright yellow numbers say "£1.99". The Tasty Burger logo, a red smile, is in the top corner.

In a shopping centre, a young woman gives free samples of Glow face cream. She is smiling and holding a white pot. She stands in front of a big pink poster with the Glow logo. In big letters, the poster says, "Try it today. Free!"

This radio advert for Harbour Fish & Chips begins with the sound of waves and seagulls. Then a friendly man's voiceover says, "Hungry? Come down to the harbour." We hear fish frying in hot oil. The voiceover tells listeners about the Friday offer: fish and chips for two for just £12. The advert ends with the address and a jingle.

This charity poster for Second Chance dog rescue shows a thin brown dog behind a metal gate. His big, sad eyes look straight at the camera. The background is dark grey. Under the photo, white letters say, "£3 a month gives Max a home." At the bottom, there is the charity's website and a small picture of a happy dog.

This online advert for ClearSkin face wash shows two photos of the same teenage boy. In the first photo, his skin is red and covered in painful spots. In the second photo, two weeks later, his skin is clear and he is smiling happily. The advert claims, "Clear skin in fourteen days." It appears on websites and apps for teenagers.

This leaflet for Greenway supermarket comes through the door on Monday. The front page is bright green and full of photos of apples, bananas and strawberries. Big red letters say, "Buy one get one free on all fruit this week!" Inside, there are more bargains on bread, eggs and milk. The supermarket's address and opening times are on the back.

This magazine advert for Velour perfume shows a woman in a long, shiny gold dress. She is standing on the stairs of a large, old house. The lighting is soft and warm, and the background is dark. In the bottom corner, there is a product shot of the glass bottle. The only words are "Velour. Paris." in thin gold letters.

In this social media video, a popular cooking influencer makes chips in a Nimbus air fryer. She talks to her two million followers like old friends. She says, "No oil, and they're even crispier than before!" She eats one and closes her eyes. Under the video, followers ask lots of questions, and she replies that the air fryer cleans easily.

In this TV commercial for Brightwhite teeth strips, a young woman looks at her yellow teeth in a mirror. Then we see her using the strips for a week. At the end, she smiles, and her teeth are much whiter. A voiceover says, "Whiter teeth in seven days, or your money back." The box appears right next to her smile.

This poster for Orbit trainers shows a product shot of one silver trainer on a black background. It seems to float in the air like a spaceship. Under it, white letters say, "Limited edition: only 500 pairs." The poster is in shopping centres near skate parks, and it shows a famous young skater's signature on the side of the shoe.

In this TV commercial for Kidz Kingdom toy shop, excited children run through the big shop and pick up toys. Everything is bright and colourful. A catchy jingle plays: "Kidz Kingdom, where the fun begins!" A cartoon crown tells viewers that every toy comes with a free gift this month. The commercial is shown on Saturday mornings during children's cartoons.

This online advert for StayEasy shows photos of a hotel room with a big bed and a beautiful view of the blue sea. Next to the photos, there are five gold stars and short reviews from happy guests: "Amazing view!" and "Great value for money." Under the reviews, the advert says the price is only £49 a night, including breakfast.

This billboard for the Tornado vacuum cleaner shows a product shot of the bright red vacuum. Behind it, there is a picture of a small tornado lifting dust off a carpet. The headline says, "Twice as powerful as other brands." The colours of the billboard are red, black and white. The website address is at the bottom in small letters.

This radio advert for Northfield Furniture starts with loud, fast, exciting music. Then a voiceover speaks very fast: "Sofas from £199! Beds from £99! Tables from £49!" He repeats the word "bargain" three times. At the end, he says the sale finishes on Sunday and gives the shop's address. There is no other sound, only his voice and the music.

This poster shows three Riverside FC players in the team's new shirt. The shirt is blue and white, and the logo of Kestrel Bank, a golden bird, is across the front. The players are famous in the city, and they all look strong and proud. The headline says, "Our new home shirt." The price, £45, is in the bottom corner.

In this TV commercial for Shine kitchen spray, a mother cleans a very messy kitchen alone. In the next room, her husband and children are watching television. She sprays the cooker, and it shines immediately. A voiceover says, "Shine. Because Mum's got enough to do." The last shot is a product shot of the yellow bottle on a clean worktop.

This magazine advert for the Arlo car shows a silver car on an empty mountain road at sunset. The lighting is golden, and the car shines. There are no other cars or people. In small, elegant letters, the text says, "Arlo. The art of driving." The price is not shown, but a website invites readers to book a test drive.

This online advert for MealBox shows a family of four sitting around a table. They are eating pasta and laughing together at a joke. Next to the photo, the advert says, "Dinner for four for £10." Below that, a box shows all the fresh ingredients that come in every delivery. The advert appears on websites about cooking and saving money.

This charity advert for the Blue Sea Trust begins with a close-up of a sea turtle. A plastic bag is caught around its neck, and it cannot swim properly. The music is very slow and sad. A quiet voiceover says, "Every year, millions of tonnes of plastic go into our seas." At the end, a website asks viewers to donate.

This leaflet for Sparrow Language School has photos of students from different countries in a bright, modern classroom. Under each photo, there is a short review: "I passed my exam!" and "The teachers are so kind." The leaflet claims that ninety per cent of students pass. On the back, there are course prices and a map of the town centre.

This poster for Crunch protein bars shows a man with huge muscles in a dark gym. He is lifting heavy weights, and his face looks serious and strong. Next to him, a product shot shows the black and red wrapper. The headline says, "Built for real men." In small letters, the poster claims each bar has twenty grams of protein.

In this social media video, an influencer opens a box of Halo headphones. She lifts them out slowly and says, "These are amazing." Then she reads comments from her followers and answers their questions. She tells them the first fifty followers who use her name in the shop will get a free headphone case. The video has thousands of likes.

In this TV commercial for Duo phones, two phones are tested side by side. One is the new Duo, and the other is a rival phone with no name. Both phones are dropped into water. The Duo still works, but the other phone does not. A voiceover claims, "Duo. Tougher than the rest." A final product shot ends the advert.

In the window of Bloom, a fashion shop, there are three shop dummies in warm winter coats: red, green and grey. Snowflakes made of paper hang above them. A big sign says, "Winter coats: buy one, get one half price!" A smaller sign says the sale ends this weekend. Through the window, shoppers are trying on scarves, gloves and hats.

This radio advert for Cosy Café begins with the sound of a coffee machine and gentle piano music. A woman's warm voiceover says, "Take a break. You deserve it." We hear cups and quiet conversation in the background. The voiceover tells listeners about the delicious new cinnamon cake. A short jingle ends the advert: "Cosy Café, your time to relax."

This poster for Bella Pizza shows a product shot of one slice of pizza on a black background. Someone is lifting the slice, and the cheese is melting and stretching. Strong lighting from above makes the cheese and tomatoes shine. There is a close-up of a green basil leaf. At the bottom, small letters say, "Bella. Hot from our oven."

This pop-up appears while a student is reading an online newspaper. It is for SkyHop, an airline. There is a photo of the Eiffel Tower at night, covered in lights. Big white letters say, "Weekend sale: Paris from £39!" A small line says that prices are for one way only. There is a bright blue button that says "Book now".

In this TV commercial for Granny's Kitchen soup, it is a cold, rainy evening. A grandmother opens the door to her wet grandchildren. She smiles warmly and gives them bowls of hot, red tomato soup. The children's faces look happy and relaxed. The kitchen is warm, with soft yellow light. At the end, a product shot shows the soup tin.

This magazine advert for Trek watches shows a climber on a frozen waterfall. Ice covers her jacket and gloves, but she is smiling. There is a product shot of the big black watch on her wrist. The text says, "Waterproof to 100 metres. Guaranteed for ten years." In small letters, it claims that the watch works at minus forty degrees.

This billboard for Comet broadband shows a cartoon comet flying across a dark blue night sky. It leaves a long, bright orange line behind it. The slogan says, "The fastest internet in town." Under the slogan, smaller letters say, "Faster than any other provider." The price, £20 a month, and a phone number are at the bottom of the billboard.

This charity leaflet for St Mary's children's hospital has two photos of a girl called Amira. In the first photo, she is in a hospital bed and looks tired and pale. In the second photo, she is smiling and playing football with her friends. The text says, "Thanks to you, Amira is home." A form inside asks readers to donate.

In this social media video, a fitness influencer talks about the PowerFit app. She shows her followers before and after photos of people who use it. One man has lost ten kilos. Then she reads a review from a follower: "Best app ever!" At the end, she says, "Download it today and start your journey." The video lasts twenty seconds.

This poster for The Royal Palms hotel shows a swimming pool at night. Gold lighting shines from under the water, and tall palm trees stand around the pool. A waiter is carrying two drinks on a shiny silver tray. There are no children or families in the picture. At the bottom, elegant gold letters say, "The Royal Palms. Five-star luxury."

In this TV commercial for PetSafe insurance, a sad, sick dog lies on a table at the vet. Its owner's face looks very worried. Then the advert jumps forward, and the dog is running happily in the park. A voiceover says, "PetSafe pays the vet's bills, guaranteed." At the end, the price, from £6 a month, appears on the screen.

This box of Holly's chocolates is dark red and covered in gold stars. In the middle, there is a picture of a snowy little village at night. Gold letters on the lid say, "Limited edition: Christmas only." The box is tied with a wide gold ribbon. On the back, a list shows the twenty different chocolates inside. It costs £12.

This online advert for Mr Fix phone repair shows a phone with a badly broken screen. Next to it, the same phone is fixed and shiny. Under the photos, there are five bright orange stars and a review: "Fixed in thirty minutes!" The advert says, "Screens fixed from £29." It appears when people search for phone repairs on the internet.

This radio advert for Sterling Cars begins with the sound of a car engine. Then a man's voiceover says, "This weekend only at Sterling Cars!" He tells listeners that everyone who buys a car before Sunday gets free insurance for one year. Then he says the shop's address twice, slowly. The advert ends with a car horn and a jingle.

This poster shows hundreds of runners in the City Marathon. Above them, there are orange flags with the PowerUp sports drink logo. One smiling runner at the front is drinking from an orange bottle. The headline says, "PowerUp: proud to support the City Marathon." Under the headline, the poster gives the date of the race and a website for runners.

In this TV commercial for Wonder Toys, boys in blue T-shirts play with toy trucks and robots in a sandpit. In a pink bedroom, girls brush their dolls' hair and make tea. A catchy jingle plays: "Wonder Toys, for girls and boys!" At the end, all the children wave at the camera. The commercial is shown during Saturday morning cartoons.

This leaflet for FitHouse gym shows two young friends laughing together on running machines. The headline says, "Bring a friend: two memberships for the price of one!" Under the photo, there is a list of classes, from yoga to boxing. The offer is for new members aged eighteen to thirty. The gym's address and phone number are on the back.

This magazine advert for Starlight jewellers shows a product shot of one diamond ring. The background is completely black. A single beam of light shines on the ring, so the diamond sparkles. There are no people in the advert. Under the ring, small silver letters say, "Starlight. For ever." There is no price, only a shop address in central London.

In this online video for the ScrubPro sponge, a smiling man holds up a burnt pan. It is black, dirty and very old. A voiceover says, "Watch this." He cleans the pan with a ScrubPro for ten seconds, and it looks new. The voiceover claims, "It cleans anything in seconds!" The video ends with a price: three sponges for £5.

This billboard for Express Rail shows a fast silver train next to a busy road. On the road, hundreds of cars are not moving. The drivers look bored and angry. The train is full of people reading and relaxing. The slogan says, "London to Manchester in two hours." The billboard is next to a motorway, where drivers can see it.

In the window of PhoneHub, there are product shots of three new phones in black, white and pink. Each phone has a price card under it. A big yellow sign says, "Free case with every phone!" A small picture shows the cases in different colours. Inside the shop, a young man in a green PhoneHub T-shirt is helping a customer.

This charity poster for Give Blood shows a nurse smiling at a young man. He is giving blood in a bright, clean room, and he looks calm and relaxed. The headline says, "You could save three lives." Under the photo, the poster claims that giving blood takes less than an hour. The website and phone number are at the bottom.

In this social media video, an influencer opens a free gift from a make-up brand called Lush Lips. She tries a bright red lipstick on camera. Her face shows surprise, then a big smile. She says, "I love this colour!" Under the video, a small line says, "Gift from Lush Lips." Many followers then ask where to buy the lipstick.

In this TV commercial for MealBox, a dad is cooking dinner. Smoke comes out of the pan, and the food is black. His children look at him and laugh. Then a MealBox arrives at the door. A voiceover says, "Even Dad can cook with MealBox." The family eat together, and the last shot is a product shot of the box.

This poster for the Summer Sound festival shows a big crowd dancing in front of a stage at sunset. Coloured lights shine above them in the sky. At the top, the words "sponsored by Fizz" are in large yellow letters, with the Fizz logo. The poster lists the bands and the dates in July. Tickets cost £60 for the weekend.

This online advert for ValueMart supermarket shows two boxes of cornflakes side by side. One is ValueMart's own brand, and the other is a famous competitor. The two boxes look almost exactly alike. Under them, the prices are £1.40 and £2.80. The headline says, "Same taste. Half the price." A green button at the bottom says, "Find your nearest store."

This radio advert for Snip hair salon is a conversation between two friends. One friend says, "I love your hair! Where did you go?" The other replies, "Snip, on the high street. It was so cheap!" Then a voiceover says that a haircut costs only £15 on weekdays. The advert ends with the salon's phone number and a short jingle.

This magazine advert for Maison Noir shows a model holding a small black leather handbag. Her facial expression is serious, and she does not smile. The background is plain, bright white, so the bag stands out. Gold letters at the bottom say, "Only 100 made." There is no price and no other text, only the brand name at the top.

This leaflet for Pronto Pizza has a photo of a large pepperoni pizza and a plate of hot garlic bread. The headline says, "Free garlic bread with every large pizza!" Under the photo, there is a short menu with prices. A large pizza costs only £11. The leaflet gives the phone number and says that delivery takes about thirty minutes.

This advert for Ripple trainers shows a teenage girl running through a rainy city at night. A close-up of her muddy shoes fills the bottom of the poster. The colours are dark blue and grey, but her trainers are bright orange, so they stand out. The slogan, "Nothing stops you", uses direct address to speak to the reader. Underneath, a call to action says, "Run today." The target audience is teenagers who never give up.
right1: The contrast between the orange trainers and the dark city draws attention to the product.
right2: The rain and mud suggest the trainers are tough enough for any running conditions.
right3: Using "you" in the slogan makes the reader feel the advert is speaking to them.
wrong1: The slogan uses a rhetorical question to make readers think about their own goals.
wrong2: The call to action creates urgency by telling readers the special offer ends today.
wrong3: The orange trainers blend into the dark background, so the girl seems part of the city.

statement: This charity advert on television begins in silence. A young boy in a dusty village walks for two hours to collect water, and the camera follows him in one long shot. Then a calm female voiceover quietly says, "Every day, millions of children make this journey." At the end, the screen turns white and shows the charity's logo and a website. The final line is an imperative: "Give £5 today and change one child's day."
right1: The long, silent walk makes viewers feel the boy's tiredness, which creates a strong emotional appeal.
right2: The voiceover's huge number shows that the problem is much bigger than one boy's story.
right3: The final imperative gives viewers one simple action and makes the cost seem small and possible.
wrong1: The final line is a rhetorical question that asks viewers what they would do in his place.
wrong2: The single long shot makes the journey feel quick, so the problem seems easy to solve.
wrong3: The calm voiceover is mainly aimed at children, who are the advert's most important target audience.

statement: In this sponsored post, a popular gaming influencer sits at her gaming desk wearing Echo headphones. She smiles at the camera and says, "I've tried every brand, and these are the best." Below the video, the caption reads, "Game louder. Win more. #EchoSquad". A small "Ad" label appears in the top corner. Many of the comments underneath ask where to buy them, and the influencer replies with a special discount code that ends on Friday.
right1: Her claim to have tried every brand is meant to make her opinion sound like an expert's.
right2: The hashtag invites followers to join a group, so buying the headphones feels like joining in.
right3: A discount code that ends on Friday creates urgency and pushes followers to buy quickly.
wrong1: The superlative "louder" in the caption claims these are the loudest headphones you can buy.
wrong2: Because the post has no label, many followers might not realise that it is really an advert.
wrong3: Her smile at the camera keeps a professional distance between the influencer and her followers.

statement: This billboard for Sunny Days orange juice looks like a faded old photograph. A family is having breakfast in a kitchen from the 1980s, with bright yellow walls, a striped tablecloth and an old radio on the table. The tagline says, "Tastes like it always did." In the bottom corner, there is a packshot of the carton next to fresh oranges. The small print explains that the juice now contains much less sugar than before.
right1: The 1980s kitchen creates nostalgia, reminding adult shoppers of happy breakfasts from their own childhood.
right2: The tagline suggests the brand has never changed, which may make it feel safe and trustworthy.
right3: Putting fresh oranges next to the carton links the product in our minds with natural, healthy fruit.
wrong1: The tagline uses alliteration so that shoppers remember the brand name when they are in a shop.
wrong2: The small print admits the juice has more sugar now, so the advert quietly hides a weakness.
wrong3: The radio on the table plays the brand's jingle, which helps people remember the advert later.

statement: In this online advert for the LingoLeap app, a teenage boy stands in a café in Madrid. In the first scene, he points nervously at the menu and looks confused and embarrassed. Then the words "Thirty days later" appear, and he orders confidently in Spanish while the waiter laughs at his joke. A voiceover asks, "What could you say in thirty days?" The advert ends with the app's logo and a green "Download free" button.
right1: The before and after scenes show the app's benefit in a way that viewers understand immediately.
right2: The voiceover's rhetorical question encourages viewers to imagine their own progress after thirty days.
right3: The waiter's laugh suggests the app helps people make real connections, not just order food.
wrong1: His confident ordering in the first scene shows that the app works from the very first day.
wrong2: The voiceover's imperative tells viewers exactly what they need to do next to start learning.
wrong3: The advert creates urgency by warning viewers that the free download ends at midnight tonight.

statement: This magazine advert for Aurum watches is printed mostly in black and gold. A man in a dark, expensive suit stands alone on the deck of a yacht at sunset, checking the time. His face is partly in shadow, but the watch is lit clearly. There is only one line of text: "For those who arrive." The brand name appears in small gold letters at the bottom of the page, and there is no price.
right1: The yacht and the suit make the watch aspirational by linking it with a wealthy lifestyle.
right2: Lighting the watch more clearly than the man's face makes the product the real focus.
right3: Leaving out the price suggests the watch is exclusive, for people who never need to ask.
wrong1: The detailed text explains the watch's features, giving readers sensible, practical reasons to buy it.
wrong2: The man's clear, smiling face invites readers to trust him as if he were a friend.
wrong3: The tagline works as a call to action, telling readers to go and buy the watch today.

statement: This public service advert on television shows a teenage boy walking home from school alone. He is looking down at his phone and smiling at a message. He steps onto the road without looking. Suddenly, we hear brakes screaming, and the screen goes black. There is silence for three seconds. Then white words appear: "Look up. It only takes a second." The advert was made by the city council and is shown before evening films.

This billboard for Pip's Pies shows a large golden pie on an old wooden kitchen table. Steam is rising from the pie, and a large piece has been cut out so we can see the chicken and mushroom filling inside. The colour palette is warm: brown, orange and cream. The tagline, in big hand-written letters, says, "Pie-fect for lunch." Underneath, a much smaller line says that the pies are baked fresh every morning in Yorkshire.

In a popular action film, the hero has just escaped from a burning building. He sits on the back of an ambulance, tired and covered in dust. A paramedic hands him a cold can of Volt cola. He drinks it slowly, and the red label faces the camera for several seconds. The actor is one of the most famous stars in the world. The brand name is never spoken, and there is no advert break.

This social media campaign for Dash trainers began with a short video of a famous dancer. She performs a simple dance in a car park wearing white Dash trainers, then says, "Your turn. #DanceWithDash." Within a week, thousands of teenagers had copied the dance and posted their own videos with the hashtag. Many of them wear Dash trainers too. The original video has been watched forty million times, and news websites have written about it.

This magazine advert for Serene face cream shows a close-up of a woman's face. Her skin looks perfect, with no lines, spots or shadows. She is looking calmly at the reader. Next to her, a white jar sits on a smooth, flat grey stone. The headline says, "Our most advanced cream ever." At the bottom of the page, in very small print, are the words "Results may vary. Based on a study of 40 women."

This TV advert is part of a new campaign for Brew coffee. It shows different people on a busy weekday morning: a nurse finishing a night shift, a student late for a lecture, and a builder on a cold, windy roof. Each person drinks a cup of Brew and says the same two words: "Wake up." At the end, the tagline appears: "Brew. Wake up to more." The advert is shown early in the morning.

This online advert appears at the bottom of a news article. It shows a photo of a smiling woman holding up an old pair of very large jeans. The headline says, "Doctors hate this one simple trick!" When readers click on it, they arrive at a page selling SlimLeaf tea. The page uses words like "miracle" and "shocking". In grey letters at the bottom, it says the tea should be used with diet and exercise.

This radio advert for Fairway Bank begins with the sound of coins dropping into a glass jar. A calm, friendly voiceover says, "Do you want to save for something special?" She explains that young people can open a savings account with just one pound. Then she says the bank's new slogan slowly and clearly: "Save smart, spend safe." Soft guitar music plays quietly in the background, and the advert ends with the bank's website address.

This bag of Kale Kick crisps is bright green, with a drawing of fresh, dark kale leaves on the front. Big white letters across the top say, "The healthiest crisp in Britain." Under these words, there is a packshot of the crisps in a simple wooden bowl. Words such as "natural", "fresh" and "goodness" appear on the back of the bag. The nutrition table on the side shows that each small bag contains 150 calories.

This Christmas advert for Hollins supermarket begins with an old man looking out of a window at the falling snow. He is alone, holding an old photo of his family. Then, suddenly, the doorbell rings. His daughter and grandchildren are standing outside, holding bags of food from Hollins. Slow piano music plays as they hug him and cook a big dinner together. At the end, the tagline appears in gold: "Christmas is better together. Hollins."

This poster for Comfy Step shoes shows a nurse in a blue uniform standing in a hospital corridor. She is smiling and pointing at her new white shoes. Next to her, there is a quote in large letters: "Twelve hours on my feet, and no pain." Under the quote, it says, "Sarah, nurse, Manchester." At the bottom, the poster asks, "Are you on your feet all day?" The poster appears in hospitals and train stations.

At the checkout in this supermarket, there is a long shelf of sweets and chocolate bars right beside the till. The packets are bright red, yellow and purple, and they are at the height of a small child's eyes. Some packets have famous cartoon characters from children's films on them. A small sign above the shelf says, "Treat yourself!" Everything costs less than a pound. While their parents pay, many children pick up a packet.

This billboard for the Vista family car shows a mother, a father and two young children driving along a quiet country road towards a lake. The sun is rising, and the sky is pink and gold. The children are laughing in the back seat, and a happy dog has its head out of the window. The car is clean, shiny and silver. The tagline says, "More room for what matters." The price begins at £24,000.

In this sponsored post, a beauty influencer with long, curly hair sits in front of a ring light. She holds up a small green bottle of Kiwi hair oil and says, "I've used this every day for six months, and look at my curls!" She runs her fingers through her hair. The caption says, "#ad Kiwi changed my hair routine. Link in my bio for 20% off." Her post has 300,000 likes and many comments.

This TV advert for Edge razors takes place in a dark bathroom with steel-grey walls. A tall, muscular man with no shirt shaves in front of a mirror. The music is loud and fast, with heavy drums. Each time he moves the razor, there is a sound like a sword. A deep male voiceover says, "Edge. The sharpest shave a man can get." The advert finishes with a packshot of the black and silver razor.

This poster for the Quit Now campaign shows a pair of human lungs on a plain white background. The lungs are grey and black, and they look damaged and dry. Above them, a headline in red capital letters says, "This is what smoking does." At the bottom, the poster says, "Stop today. Call our free, friendly helpline." The campaign is run by the government, and the posters appear in bus stops and doctors' waiting rooms.

This online advert for SkyHop appears when someone searches for flights to Rome. It shows a photo of a sunny square with an old stone fountain. Red letters flash at the top: "Only 3 seats left at this price!" Below, the price says, "Rome from £59." A large, bright orange button says, "Book now." In small grey print under the button, the advert says that bags cost extra and that prices change every few hours.

This TV advert for Volley sportswear shows a famous tennis player during the final point of a big match. Everything happens in slow motion: the ball, the sweat on her face, and the crowd jumping up. She wins and falls slowly to her knees. The camera moves closer to the Volley logo on her shirt. Then the slogan appears in white letters on a black screen: "Never stop." There is no voiceover, only the crowd.

This poster for the Pixel Retro games console looks like an old video game from the 1990s. The pictures are made of big, square pixels, and the colours are bright purple and green. A small cartoon character jumps over a mushroom. The headline asks, "Remember 1995?" Underneath, the poster says that the console has fifty classic games inside. The posters appear in train stations at rush hour, where most travellers are adults going to work.

This magazine advert for Bean There coffee shows a small brown paper loyalty card on a café table. Nine of the ten circles on the card have been stamped with a coffee cup. Next to the card, there is a cup of coffee with a heart drawn in the milk. The headline says, "Your tenth coffee is on us." At the bottom, the advert says, "Pick up your card in any Bean There café today."

This poster at a bus stop is for Frosty ice lollies. It shows a packshot of three lollies, orange, pink and blue, sitting in a pile of ice. Drops of water run down them. The headline says, "Meltdown Monday: two for one, today only!" The poster has a timer in the corner, and it only appears on Mondays when the temperature is over twenty-five degrees. A small map at the bottom shows the nearest shop.

This TV advert for the Volta electric car shows a woman driving on a long, empty road through the desert. She stops at a small charging station in the middle of nowhere, next to a café. While her car charges, she buys a coffee. Before she finishes it, a sound tells her the car is ready. Then the tagline appears: "Fully charged in ten minutes." The final shot shows the car driving into the sunset.

This advert appears on a popular food delivery app used by students in Shanghai. It is for ChaCha bubble tea. At the top, there is a photo of two tall cups of brown sugar milk tea with ice. Red Chinese and English words say, "Second cup ¥1, today only!" Under the photo, there is the hashtag #ChaChaTime and a small timer showing how many hours are left. A big, round red button says, "Order now."

This poster for the Clean Streets campaign shows a city pavement covered in rubbish: drink cans, crisp packets and coffee cups. In the middle of the poster, there is a clean green bin. Large black letters say, "Bin it. Don't drop it." Under this, smaller letters say, "Bin it for your street. Bin it for your city." The poster was made by the local council for this summer and appears in parks and shopping streets.

This TV advert for Swift swimwear shows an Olympic swimmer training alone in an empty pool before sunrise. The water is very still, and the only light comes from the pool. She dives in and swims very fast. When she stops, the camera shows the Swift logo on her swimming cap. A voiceover says, "Swift is proud to sponsor Team GB." The advert ends with a website where viewers can buy the same blue swimsuit.

This online advert for the mobile game Kingdom Clash shows a huge battle between two cartoon armies. Giant dragons fly above the castles, and orange fire lights up the sky. Big gold letters say, "10 million players can't be wrong." Underneath, the advert shows that the game has 4.8 stars from over a million reviews. A green button says, "Download free and join the battle." The advert appears inside other games and on video websites.

This magazine advert for the Azure Bay resort shows an empty beach with white sand and turquoise sea. A single wooden chair sits under a tall palm tree, facing the water. There are no people in the photo. The colour palette is white, turquoise and pale gold. Across the sky, elegant gold letters say, "Your escape is waiting." At the bottom, a small line gives the resort's website and the words "Seven nights from £1,200."

This billboard for the Wave mobile network shows a map of the whole country covered in bright blue. In front of the map, a young man is making a video call to his family from the top of a mountain. The headline says, "100% coverage*". Next to the star, at the bottom of the billboard, very small print explains that the figure is for towns and cities only. The billboard stands beside a busy road.

This TV advert for Starla dolls takes place in a pink bedroom with pink curtains and a pink carpet. Three girls sit on the bed, brushing the long blonde hair of their dolls and choosing sparkly dresses and shoes for them. A soft, sweet song plays: "Starla, Starla, pretty as a star." At the end, all the girls hold up their dolls and smile sweetly. The advert is shown during children's programmes on Saturday morning.

This charity poster for Shelter Now shows a man sleeping in a shop doorway at night. He is wrapped in an old grey blanket, and his shoes are next to him. In the photo, the legs of busy shoppers walk past him, but nobody stops or looks down. A white question appears in the middle: "Would you walk past?" At the bottom, it says, "£10 gives someone a warm bed tonight. Text BED to 70070."

This box of Hearth granola has a hand-drawn picture of a small farm on the front. There is a red barn, a field of ripe wheat, a few chickens and a farmer's kitchen with an open window. The words "homemade" and "golden" appear in brown, hand-written letters. On the back, there is a short story about the farmer's grandmother and her original recipe. The box is made of plain brown card, and it costs £4.50.

This TV advert for Loyal dog food begins with a young boy getting a small puppy for his birthday. Then we watch the boy and the dog grow up together: playing in the garden, going to school, and later sitting together on the sofa. At the end, the man is grown up, and the dog is old and grey. The tagline says, "Loyal. Fifteen years of friendship." The advert has no words until the end.

This online video for Surge energy drink shows a cyclist riding at full speed across the roof of a tall building. He jumps across the gap to another roof, lands safely, and keeps going without stopping. The video looks like it was filmed on a phone, and it has no music. At the end, he opens a can of Surge. It was posted with #SurgeOn, and it was shared millions of times in two days.

This poster for Northgate University shows five smiling students sitting on the grass in front of an old stone building. They come from many different countries, and they are laughing together at something on a phone. One is holding a laptop, and another is holding a cup of coffee. The headline says, "Your future starts here." At the bottom, the poster gives the date of the next open day and says, "Find your course today."

This online advert for PriceRight supermarket shows a full shopping basket on a white background. In the basket, there are fresh vegetables, a loaf of bread, a bottle of milk and two bags of pasta. The colour palette is bright orange and white. Above the basket, orange letters say, "The lowest prices in town." Under the basket, it says, "Full basket: only £15." A button says, "Shop online now." The advert appears on cooking websites.

This TV advert for Lumi perfume shows a beautiful young couple walking along an empty beach at sunset. Their white clothes move in the wind, and the light is soft and golden. They look into each other's eyes and laugh, but they never speak. Slow, dreamy music plays, and the waves wash over their feet. At the end, there is a packshot of the glass bottle on the sand, and a soft voice says, "Lumi."

This radio advert for the Summer Sound festival begins with a huge crowd cheering and loud rock music. Then an excited voiceover says, "Summer Sound is back!" She lists the famous bands that will play this year, one after another. Then she says, "Tickets on sale Friday at nine. Friday at nine. Don't miss it: Friday at nine!" Last year, all the tickets sold out in two hours. The advert ends with the festival's website.

This poster for the new Kite phone shows a photo of a quiet city street late at night. The photo is bright and clear, and you can see every star in the sky. In the bottom corner, there is a packshot of the black phone. A small line under the photo says, "Shot on Kite." The tagline says, "See the dark." The poster claims that no other phone takes photos like this in the dark.

This TV advert for Sparkle floor cleaner shows a mother mopping a kitchen floor while her children run in with muddy football boots. She smiles and cleans the floor again in a few seconds. A voiceover says, "Nine out of ten mums recommend Sparkle." Then three other women speak to the camera and say how easy it is to use. The last shot is a packshot of the bright purple bottle on the shiny floor.

This online advert for Trendy, a fast fashion shop, shows a row of clothes moving across the screen: jeans, crop tops, jackets and trainers. Each item has a small price under it, from only £5 to £20. Big pink letters say, "New in every day." Under the clothes, a small line says, "Free delivery when you order in the next hour." The advert appears on the social media apps that many teenagers use every day.

This billboard for FitHouse gym appears in January. It shows a young woman running on a treadmill. She looks strong, fit and happy, and she is not tired. Behind her, there is a large window with a view of the city. The tagline, in big white letters, says, "New year. New you." Under the tagline, the billboard says, "Join this month and pay nothing until February." The gym's logo is a small, bright orange flame.

This poster for Fair Leaf chocolate shows a cocoa farmer called Ama standing in a green field on her farm in Ghana. She is smiling and holding a pile of cocoa beans in her hands. Next to her, there is a quote: "I grew the cocoa in this chocolate." A packshot of the chocolate bar sits at the bottom of the poster. The words "fair", "honest" and "proud" appear on the wrapper in large letters.

This social media post for Peak Outdoor shows a woman walking alone on a snowy mountain. She is wearing a grey jacket, a green hat and green boots, and she carries a small backpack. Like every post from this brand, the colours are grey, green and white, and there are no bright colours. The caption says, "Some paths are worth the climb. #GoFurther." The post has no prices and no links to products for sale.

These screens in a Shanghai metro station show an advert for a shopping app's Double 11 sale. Huge red numbers count down on a gold background: "3 days left!" The same advert appears on every screen along the platform. Each time the train arrives, the advert changes to show a different product: phones, shoes and rice cookers. At the end of each advert, a voice says, "Open the app and add to your basket now!"

This two-page magazine feature looks like an ordinary article. Its title is "My week without sugar", and it is written in the first person by a busy mother of two from Leeds who describes her tiredness, her cravings and her surprise at how much better she felt. Halfway through, she mentions that she started every morning with a bowl of Pure Oats. The body copy includes facts about fibre and slow-release energy. Only a small grey label in the top corner, reading "Promotion", shows that the brand paid for it.

On a popular news website, an article titled "Ten best cities for working from home" appears between stories about politics and sport. It has exactly the same font, layout and style of photos as the other articles on the website's front page. Each city is described with beautiful, sunny images of cafés and beaches, and every description ends with the cost of a return flight. At the bottom, a line reads, "In partnership with SkyHop." The airline's logo appears only once, and there is no direct instruction to book anything.

One Monday morning, people walking through a busy shopping street in Manchester notice giant white footprints painted on the grey pavement. Each print is about a metre long and shows the pattern of a trainer sole. The footprints continue for half a kilometre, around corners and up steps, until they stop outside the door of a new Stride trainer shop. There are no posters and no words, only the footprints and the brand's small logo inside the final print. Within hours, photos of the trail are all over social media.

This TV advert for Homeguard insurance begins in a dark house at night. A family is asleep upstairs. The camera slowly follows a man's shadow as it moves across the wall of a child's bedroom, while low, tense music builds. A floorboard creaks. Then the screen cuts to black, and a serious voice asks, "If the worst happened, would you be covered?" The strapline appears in white letters: "Homeguard. Sleep soundly." Finally, the voice explains that quotes take five minutes online and that new customers receive a free door alarm.

On a TV shopping channel, a presenter in a bright red jacket stands behind a shiny kitchen counter, demonstrating the Whirl blender. She speaks quickly and loudly, describing it as "the most incredible machine you will ever own". A counter in the corner of the screen shows how many blenders are left, and the number keeps falling: forty, thirty-two, twenty. Every few seconds she repeats the phone number and urges viewers to call immediately. A banner across the bottom announces that the price will rise by thirty pounds at midnight.

This full-page magazine advert for the Volta electric car contains only a small photo of the car in the top left corner. The rest of the page is body copy and tables. The text explains that the car can travel 520 kilometres on one charge, that it costs about two pence per kilometre to run, and that it has received the highest safety rating. A bar chart compares its running costs with those of a similar petrol car. Under the photo, a short caption reads, "The numbers speak for themselves."

After a university student searches online for cheap camping trips in Scotland, she begins to see adverts for Ridgeline tents on almost every website she visits. The adverts show young people laughing around a campfire under the stars, with mountains and a lake behind them. The text says, "You've been thinking about it. Now go." One advert even mentions the area she searched for. The tents are light and inexpensive, and the adverts appear mainly late in the evening, when she is most likely to be browsing on her phone.

This TV advert for Clearwell still water shows a woman doing yoga on the edge of a cliff at sunrise. The sea is calm below her, and the only sounds are waves and birds. She moves slowly and breathes deeply. A tall glass bottle of Clearwell stands beside her mat, catching the light, but she never opens it or drinks from it. There is no voiceover. At the very end, a few words appear in a thin, white font: "Clearwell. Find your stillness." The brand donates to ocean protection charities.

This billboard for Crunchers crisps shows a man in a smart suit who has just dropped an entire bag of crisps on the floor of a busy, open-plan office during a meeting. His colleagues are staring at him, and his face is frozen in horror. Crisps are scattered everywhere. Above the scene, huge orange letters announce: "Avoid a snackcident." Underneath, in smaller letters, the billboard adds, "Crunchers. Now in a resealable bag." A packshot of the new bag, with its zip at the top, appears in the bottom right corner.

This government poster against drink-driving shows a car that has crashed into a tree on a dark, wet country road. The front of the car is completely crushed, and broken glass covers the road. The photo is lit by the blue lights of an emergency vehicle. On the back seat, we can see a small pink child's shoe. There are no people anywhere in the picture. The strapline, in plain white letters, says, "One more drink isn't worth it." The poster appears in pubs, bars and petrol stations in December.

This magazine advert for Serene foundation shows a close-up of a model's face. Her skin is completely smooth and even, without a single line, pore or freckle, and it seems to glow. Her eyes look directly at the reader, and her lips are slightly open. The headline claims, "Flawless skin in one step." Beside the bottle, a list of ingredients is described as "advanced". At the very bottom of the page, in tiny grey print that is difficult to read, a line says, "Image digitally enhanced. Model wears additional products."

In this TV advert for Bloom skincare, a well-known actress sits in a bright, simple bathroom in the early morning. At first, she is wearing no make-up, and her hair is tied back simply. Speaking softly, almost in a whisper, she tells the viewer about her morning routine as she gently applies the cream. She does not mention price or offers. Instead, she says, "I've trusted Bloom for ten years." At the end, the brand name appears, followed by the words "Bloom ambassador since 2016". Calm piano music plays throughout.

This poster announces a new look for Bun & Go, a burger chain that has existed since the 1990s. The old red and yellow logo has been replaced with a simple dark green circle and the brand name in lowercase white letters. The photo shows a single burger on plain brown paper, surrounded by fresh green lettuce, tomatoes and herbs. The strapline says, "Fresh is back." Underneath, the body copy explains that the chain now uses local beef and paper packaging. The menu, however, has hardly changed since last year.

This advert appears in a small magazine for people who collect fountain pens. It shows a single photograph of a dark blue fountain pen lying on a sheet of handwritten paper. Below the photo, a long paragraph explains how each Inkwell pen is made by hand in a workshop in Edinburgh, how long it takes to shape the gold nib, and which wood is used for the case. The language is calm, careful and detailed. The price, £480, is given clearly at the end, along with the workshop's postal address.

This TV advert for ValueMart supermarket shows dozens of different shoppers filling their trolleys to a cheerful, catchy song. There is a student buying pasta, an elderly couple choosing fruit, a young dad with twins, and a group of teenagers buying snacks for a party. Everyone is smiling; nobody looks stressed. The camera moves quickly from one person to the next. Price labels pop up beside the products. The strapline appears at the end: "ValueMart. Good food for everyone." The advert is shown at peak times on the main channels.

This short online video shows a puppy chasing a Robo robot vacuum cleaner around a living room. Every time the puppy gets close, the robot turns away, and the puppy falls over its own feet. It looks like home footage filmed on a phone. There is no voiceover and no music, just the sound of the puppy barking and someone laughing. The brand name appears only once, on top of the robot. The video has been shared millions of times, and many viewers did not realise it was an advert.

This poster for the Living Forest charity shows a large photo of an empty brown field under a grey sky. There are a few tree stumps and some deep tyre tracks in the mud, and nothing else. Without words, the image could be any field in the countryside. However, a single caption at the bottom changes its meaning: "This was a forest last year." Under the caption, a smaller line asks readers to sponsor a tree for £5. The poster is printed on recycled paper and displayed in railway stations.

During one week, twenty small influencers, each with between five and fifty thousand followers, post photos using Kiwi hair oil. They are not famous, and their posts look like ordinary moments from their lives: a morning routine, a gym bag, a messy bathroom shelf. Every post includes the same discount code, KIWI15, and most speak to followers in a casual, friendly way, such as "OK guys, you have to try this." Some posts include "#ad" at the end of the caption, but several do not mention a partnership at all.

This radio advert for the LuckySpin betting app begins with the sound of a crowd cheering at a football match. An excited voiceover shouts that new customers who sign up today can receive £50 in free bets. He repeats the offer twice and tells listeners to download the app right now before the weekend's matches. Then, in the last few seconds, a different voice reads a long legal disclaimer extremely quickly: "Over eighteens only. Terms apply. When the fun stops, stop." The disclaimer is almost impossible for listeners to understand.

This TV advert for Fairway Bank shows a young couple sitting at a kitchen table with a laptop, looking at their savings. A calm, clear voiceover explains the bank's new account: an interest rate of 4.5%, no monthly fees, and money that can be withdrawn at any time. Simple graphics show the numbers growing over five years. The couple are relaxed, and the kitchen is tidy and quiet. At the end, the strapline appears: "Fairway. Plan for tomorrow." There is no music, only the voice and some soft background sounds.

This poster for Volley sportswear shows a female sprinter at the start of a race. She has a running blade in place of her lower left leg, and she is staring down the long, empty track with total focus. The whole photo is in black and white, apart from her orange Volley vest. The strapline, in large white capitals, says, "No limits." There is no other text and no product information. The poster appears around stadiums during a major international athletics event, and the athlete is a famous Paralympic champion.

This online advert for Kicks Club shows a pair of white and gold trainers on a dark background, lit from below so that they glow. Only the outline of the brand's logo is visible. Big text says, "Members only. 100 pairs." Underneath, a countdown shows that the trainers will be released on Saturday at ten in the morning, and that only registered members can buy them. To become a member, customers must pay a yearly fee of £50. The advert appears on websites and forums read by serious trainer collectors.

In this TV advert for Bright toothpaste, a man in a white coat stands in a clean, modern laboratory. He holds up a large model of a tooth and explains, using a diagram, how the toothpaste's formula protects enamel from acid. Graphs and percentages appear on the screen beside him. He speaks seriously and clearly, like a teacher in a class. In very small text at the bottom of the screen, for less than two seconds, a line says, "Actor portrayal." The advert ends with the claim, "Recommended by dentists."

In this online video, a popular travel vlogger spends five days exploring the Greek island of Lefkada. She swims in clear blue bays, eats in small family restaurants and talks warmly about the friendly local people. The video is beautiful and relaxed, and she never asks viewers to buy anything. At the very beginning, she says quickly, "This trip was paid for by Visit Lefkada," and a small label in the corner says "Paid partnership". Many comments under the video say that they now want to visit the island too.

This magazine advert for the Barista coffee machine shows a large, bright loft apartment with high windows and white walls. A man in his thirties, wearing a casual shirt, stands by the window holding a coffee cup and looking out at the city. Everything in the room is neat and expensive: a leather sofa, a record player, a shelf of design books. The silver coffee machine sits on a white marble counter near the window. The only text is "Barista. Your mornings, perfected." The advert appears in a design magazine.

This billboard for Cloud office chairs shows a businessman asleep in a grey leather office chair that is floating high above a city. Soft white clouds surround him, and a few birds fly past his feet. He looks completely relaxed, with his tie loose and a smile on his face. The strapline, in big blue letters, says, "The most comfortable chair in the universe." Under it, smaller letters say, "Sit back. You've earned it." The billboard is placed on a busy road leading into the financial district of the city.

For one week in July, a metro station in central Shanghai is transformed into a beach by Sun Travel. Real sand covers part of the platform, and deckchairs and colourful beach umbrellas stand along the walls. The sound of waves and seagulls plays from hidden speakers. Tired commuters in suits take photos and lie in the deckchairs while they wait for trains. Small signs say, "Your holiday is closer than you think," with a code for a discount. Videos of the station have been shared widely on Chinese social media.

This TV advert for Shield antivirus software begins in a dark room where a hacker sits before several screens. His face is lit blue by the monitors, and we cannot see his eyes. Fast, nervous electronic music plays in the background. On one screen, we see a family's photos, bank details and passwords appearing one by one. A loud voice says, "Every 39 seconds, someone is hacked. Will you be next?" The strapline appears: "Shield. Don't wait until it's too late." The special offer for new customers ends on Sunday.

This new, limited edition bag of Crunchers crisps has a large badge on the front that says, "You chose this flavour!" Last summer, the brand asked the public to vote online between three new flavours, and more than a million people took part in just two weeks. The winning flavour, chilli and lime, is shown in a packshot with a bright green and red background. On the back, the body copy thanks fans for voting and invites them to suggest next year's flavour on the brand's website or social media.

This bar of Root & Branch soap is wrapped in plain brown paper and tied with natural string. There is no plastic anywhere on the packaging. A small paper label shows a simple hand-drawn tree. On the back, a short paragraph explains the brand's values: every ingredient is grown on small farms, nothing is tested on animals, and ten per cent of profits support forest projects. The language is simple and personal, ending with the words, "Thank you for choosing gently." The bar costs £7, much more than ordinary soap.

This TV advert for the Regent saloon car shows a grey-haired man in his sixties driving slowly along a coastal road at sunset. Gentle piano music plays. He is alone in the car, relaxed and smiling slightly, with one hand on the wheel. The car's interior is shown in close-up: soft leather seats, wooden panels and a quiet engine. There is no talk of speed or price. At the end, a calm male voice says, "The Regent. You've arrived." The advert is shown during evening news programmes and golf tournaments.

This magazine advert for the Wave mobile network is aimed at teenagers. It shows three friends taking a selfie together on a city rooftop at night, all laughing. The text is written as if it were a text message between friends: "No cap, Wave is lowkey the best deal rn." Below this, the body copy uses invented words such as "datastic" and "unlimitless" to describe the new unlimited phone plan. The price, £12 a month, is printed in a speech bubble, along with the line, "Ur parents will approve too."

This poster for the Quit Now campaign shows a single cigarette on a black background. However, the cigarette looks like the fuse of a bomb: the end is burning with bright orange sparks, and a thin line of smoke rises above it. There are no people or other objects in the image. Below the picture, white letters say, "Every cigarette brings it closer." Underneath, in smaller letters, there is the number of a free, confidential helpline. The posters appear on the sides of city buses and in hospital waiting rooms.

When a customer visits the website of Trendy, an online clothes shop, a bright pop-up appears immediately with a red countdown timer: "Offer ends in 09:59." The pop-up promises 40% off absolutely everything if the customer orders before the timer reaches zero. The numbers tick down second by second, and a message underneath says, "23 people are looking at this item right now." However, if the customer reloads the page, the timer starts again from ten minutes. Several consumer groups have already complained about the website to the advertising regulator.

This page in a weekend newspaper looks like a normal health article. Its headline asks, "Are you getting enough vitamins this winter?" The article interviews a nutrition expert and describes how tiredness, low mood and colds are common in the dark winter months. Near the end, it recommends Vita gummies, describing them as "the easy way to stay healthy". A photo shows the colourful, fruit-shaped sweets in a glass bowl. At the bottom, small text says "Advertisement feature", and a line warns that supplements should not replace a varied diet.

This two-minute TV advert for Lumi perfume is like a short film. A young woman runs through the streets of Paris at night, past glowing cafés and shop windows, across a bridge and up the stairs of an old building. She opens a door onto a rooftop full of light and music, where a group of friends welcome her. Nobody speaks, and we never learn her story. The perfume bottle is not shown until the final three seconds, when it appears on a black screen with the single word "Lumi".

This billboard for Sterling Cars is bright red and covered in large yellow letters. The main headline shouts, "0% finance! Today only!" Below it, three new cars are shown with huge prices beside them, and a starburst shape says, "Huge savings!" A huge arrow points down the road towards the garage, which is only two hundred metres away. At the bottom, in very small white text, a disclaimer explains that the offer depends on a large first payment and is only available to some customers with a good credit history.

After a young man orders fast food from a delivery app late at night several times in one week, he begins to see adverts for the FitHouse gym on his phone. One shows a fit man of his age running at dawn and says, "Tired of feeling tired?" Another shows a pair of jeans that no longer fit around the waist, with the line, "It's not too late to start." The adverts appear mostly after midnight. Each one offers a free first week and a button that says "Start tomorrow".

This magazine advert for Aurum watches shows a famous international footballer in a dark suit, sitting alone in an empty stadium at night, under the floodlights. He is looking down at the gold watch on his wrist and smiling slightly to himself. Under the photo, a paragraph of body copy describes his career: how he started playing on the streets of Lagos and became the captain of his national team. It ends with the line, "Every great moment is timed. Aurum." There is no price, only the brand's website address.

This poster introduces the new look of Fairway Bank, which has been a traditional, serious bank for over a hundred years. The old dark blue shield has gone. In its place, the name "fairway" is written in round, lowercase letters, and the "y" curves upwards like a smile. The background is bright yellow, and the logo looks almost like a cartoon. The new strapline says, "Banking that's on your side." Underneath, the body copy explains that the bank's app has been redesigned to be simpler and friendlier for young customers.

This Christmas TV advert for Hollins supermarket shows many different families preparing one meal in their own homes: a grandmother teaching her grandson to roast potatoes, two dads decorating a table, a student cooking for friends in a tiny flat, and a large Indian family making dessert. Warm, gentle music plays, and the camera moves smoothly from kitchen to kitchen. At the end, the screen splits, and all the families appear around their tables at the same time. The strapline appears in gold letters: "However you celebrate, Hollins is there."

In a popular car racing video game, players drive through a city at night at very high speed, avoiding traffic and the police. Along the road, there are huge, bright digital billboards for Volt cola, showing the red can and the brand's logo. When players pass a certain point, a Volt cola truck drives across the road. The billboards fit naturally into the game's world, and many players hardly notice them. The game is mainly played by teenagers and young adults, and it is completely free to download on phones.

This magazine advert for MaxBuild protein powder shows a man with no shirt standing in a gym. His muscles are huge and perfectly defined, and his skin is smooth and shining under strong lights. The headline says, "Gains guaranteed. Results in 30 days." A large black tub of powder stands on a bench beside him, with gold letters on the label. Next to a star at the bottom of the page, small print explains that results depend on exercise and diet. Experts say the photo has clearly been digitally changed.

This radio advert for EaseAll pain tablets begins with a tired woman sighing loudly, then describing a terrible headache that stopped her from working. A calm male voice explains that EaseAll contains ibuprofen and starts working in just fifteen minutes. He gives a few simple facts: suitable for adults, available in all chemists and supermarkets, and gentle on the stomach. At the end, he says clearly, "Always read the label. If symptoms continue, speak to your pharmacist." The final words are spoken slowly, so that every listener can hear them.

This TV advert for Crunchtastic cereal shows a family of colourful cartoon animals dancing around a kitchen table. A loud, catchy song plays, and the word "Crunchtastic" is sung again and again by different characters: the dog, the cat and even the talking toaster. Each time the word is sung, it appears in bright yellow letters on the screen. Then real children and parents are shown eating the cereal together at a sunny table and laughing. The advert is shown at breakfast time and during family programmes in the evening.

This poster for Bright Energy shows a large, simple bar chart on a white background. The bars show a typical family's electricity bill falling year by year after switching to solar panels: from £1,200 to £400. The chart is in calm shades of green and blue. Under the chart, the caption says, "This is what switching looks like." A short paragraph explains that the panels are installed in one day and come with a twenty-year guarantee. The brand's values, "clean, simple, fair", appear in small letters next to the logo.

In a livestream on a Chinese shopping app, a popular host sits in a bright pink studio surrounded by boxes of face masks. She speaks extremely quickly, holding up the product and applying one to her own face. Every few minutes she shouts, "Only five thousand left! Three, two, one, link's live!" The number of buyers flashes on the screen, rising rapidly. Comments from viewers scroll past quickly, many asking about prices and skin types. The host calls viewers "family" and promises a free gift to the first thousand customers.

This TV advert for the Ridgeback 4x4 shows a single driver crossing a huge, empty desert. There are no roads, only sand dunes, rocks and an enormous sky. The car climbs steep hills and races through a dry riverbed, sending up clouds of dust. At night, the driver sleeps on the roof under the stars. We never see a city, a road sign or another person during the whole advert. The strapline appears at the end: "Ridgeback. Go where the road ends." The advert appears during adventure and wildlife documentaries.

Above a busy crossing in a large city, a giant curved screen shows a 3D image of a huge orange cartoon cat. Because of the shape of the screen, the cat appears to climb out of the building and look down at the people below. It yawns, stretches and finally holds up a can of Purr cat food. There are no words or prices, only the brand's logo in the corner. People stop in the street to film it, and videos of the billboard have been shared millions of times.

This poster for the Run Club sportswatch shows a woman running alone along an empty city street in heavy rain. She is soaking wet, but her face is calm and focused. On her wrist, the small watch screen is glowing bright green. The photo is dark, with grey and blue tones. The only words are "Your pace." in small white letters in the top corner, and the brand's logo below. The poster appears in train stations in the early morning, when tired commuters walk past on the way to work.

This full-page magazine advert for Northern Oil is dominated by green. A row of white wind turbines stands on a hillside covered in fresh grass, and in the foreground, a child's hand holds a single bright green leaf. The headline reads, "Powering a cleaner tomorrow." The body copy describes the company's investment in renewable energy, using words such as "natural", "responsible" and "future". Only one line, near the end, mentions that solar and wind make up less than three per cent of the company's business. The company's logo, a green and yellow sunflower, sits quietly in the bottom right corner.

This poster appeared overnight on a busy bus shelter in central London. At first glance, it looks exactly like an advert for Tasty Burger, with the same red background, the same smiling logo and the same photograph of a huge, dripping cheeseburger. However, the slogan has been changed from "Grab some happy" to "Grab some heart disease". Underneath, in the brand's own font, a line of small print lists the burger's salt, sugar and fat content. The poster was made by an activist group, not the company, and photos of it spread quickly across social media within a single day.

This thirty-second TV advert for the Robo mop opens with a loud crash as a toddler knocks a bowl of cereal onto a clean white kitchen floor. The parents look at each other in complete despair.
