A voiceover asks, "Tired of cleaning the same floor three times a day?" Next, the Robo mop glides out from under a cupboard and cleans the mess in seconds while the family sit down to breakfast. The voiceover lists three features: it maps the room, it empties itself and it is controlled by a phone app. The final screen says, "Order now. Delivery tomorrow."

This TV advert for Volley sportswear follows a girls' under-fifteen football team through a muddy, rainy season. We see them training in the dark, arguing with referees and celebrating a very late winning goal. At the beginning, a boy on the touchline shouts, "You play like a girl!" as an insult. At the end, the team captain turns to the camera after scoring and repeats the phrase proudly: "Yeah. I play like a girl." The Volley logo appears on the team's shirts throughout, and the final screen shows the hashtag #LikeAGirl next to a link to the new women's collection.

This TV advert for the new Kite phone uses a split screen. On the left, a young man struggles with last year's Kite 7 model: the screen is dull, apps load slowly and the battery runs out during a video call. The colours on that side are grey and washed out. On the right, a confident young woman uses the new model, which is bright, fast and full of colour, as she films a crowded outdoor concert. A voiceover says, "Why live in the past?" The final screen shows the new phone next to a trade-in offer for older models.

This magazine advert for Aurum shows a long dinner table in an elegant restaurant, lit by candles. Eight well-dressed guests in their thirties are laughing and talking. In the centre of the image, a man reaches for his wine glass, and his heavy gold watch catches the light. Several guests are glancing at it. The man's face is not fully shown, so the watch is the real subject of the photograph. The text is minimal: "Aurum. Noticed." There is no price and no information about the watch's features, only the brand name and the address of its single London boutique.

This online advert for Peak Air shows a small aluminium can with a picture of snowy mountains on the side. A young woman in a crowded, polluted city lifts the can to her face, presses a button and breathes in deeply. Her eyes close in pleasure, and she smiles slowly. The text describes the product as "100% pure Alpine air, hand-collected at 3,000 metres". It claims the air will leave buyers feeling "refreshed, focused and alive". Each can contains about one hundred breaths and costs £14.99. The advert appears on social media in cities with high levels of air pollution.

This TV advert for Lumi perfume is filmed entirely in black and white, in the style of a 1950s Hollywood film. A woman in a long satin dress and white gloves walks slowly down a grand marble staircase as an orchestra plays dramatic music. Men in dinner suits turn to watch her. The credits at the beginning use old-fashioned curly lettering, and the picture even has small scratches, as if it were an old film reel. In the final seconds, the bottle of Lumi appears in full colour, glowing gold, while the rest of the screen stays black and white.

This TV advert for Homeguard alarm systems shows a family's house at night, seen from outside. Rain is falling, and a heavy storm is building. Inside, the parents check on their sleeping children before going to bed themselves. A small blue light glows steadily on a white box by the front door. A calm, reassuring voiceover says, "Whatever happens outside, they're safe inside." The camera then shows a phone screen, where the parents can watch every room. The advert ends with the family having breakfast together in a bright kitchen and the strapline, "Homeguard. Peace of mind, around the clock."

This online advert for Kingdom Clash does not show the game itself for most of its thirty seconds. Instead, it shows four teenage friends in different cities, each in their own bedroom, talking and laughing on a video call while they play together. One friend has just moved to a new country, and the others greet her with cheers when she joins their team. They share inside jokes and call each other by nicknames that only they understand. Only at the end does the advert show the game's colourful battle screen, followed by the line, "Wherever you are, play together."

When readers try to leave the website of a popular food magazine, a large pop-up suddenly fills the screen. It offers a subscription at £1 for the first month. The "Subscribe" button is large, bright green and in the centre of the box. Underneath, in small grey text, the option to close the pop-up says, "No thanks, I don't like saving money." Next to the green button, a small box has already been ticked for them to agree to marketing emails. In the small print, readers can see that after the first month the price rises to £12 a month.

This billboard for Bean There coffee shows a close-up of a cup of coffee on a wooden table, with steam rising and a perfect heart drawn in the milk foam. Dark roasted coffee beans are scattered around the cup, and a small chocolate sits on the saucer. Across the top, in large, elegant cream letters, the billboard claims, "The best coffee in the world." There is no evidence, award or statistic to support the claim. Underneath, a smaller line reads, "Now in over 400 cafés." The billboard is placed directly opposite a rival coffee chain on a busy shopping street.

This magazine advert for Starlight jewellers shows a dark wooden table lit only by a single candle. On the table, there is a single deep red rose and a small open box containing a diamond ring. A few rose petals lie beside it, and a glass of champagne stands in the shadows behind. The image is warm and slightly blurred at the edges, so the ring is the sharpest object in the picture. There are no people and no words except the brand's name, written in thin silver handwriting at the bottom, and the date of Valentine's Day, 14 February.

Across a whole year of TV adverts, Hollins supermarket always uses the same family. The parents are white and in their forties, with two children, a boy and a girl, and a golden retriever. They live in a large detached house with a big garden in the countryside. The mother is usually cooking, while the father lights the barbecue or carves the meat. They are always calm and well-dressed, they never argue, and their huge kitchen is spotless and full of expensive equipment. Each advert ends with the family around the table and the strapline, "Hollins. Food for every family."

This billboard originally advertised a huge three-day weekend sale at a shopping centre, with the headline "Buy more. Save more." and a photograph of smiling shoppers carrying bags. During the night, however, someone painted over two words, so that it now reads "Buy more. Be happy?" A large red question mark has been added beside the shoppers' smiling faces. The change was made by an anti-consumerism group, who also attached small stickers reading "Buy Nothing Day" around the frame. Photos of the altered billboard were shared thousands of times online before the shopping centre had it cleaned the next afternoon.

This TV advert for Rocket crisps retells the story of Little Red Riding Hood. A girl in a red cloak walks through a dark, misty forest, carrying a basket of food for her sick grandmother. When she reaches her grandmother's cottage, the wolf is in the bed, wearing a nightdress. However, when she says, "What big teeth you have!", the wolf ignores her and grabs the bag of Rocket crisps from her basket. He eats them noisily and happily and says, "Sorry, I'm not here for you." The advert ends with a packshot and the line, "Rocket. Worth the trip."

This TV advert for ValueMart's Black Friday sale begins with a crowd of people waiting outside a large store in the dark. A large digital clock counts down the final seconds to midnight. When the doors open, the shoppers rush inside, grabbing televisions, laptops and toys from the shelves. Loud, upbeat music plays, and the editing is fast and exciting. Prices with red lines through them flash across the screen, replaced by lower ones. The voiceover shouts, "Biggest deals of the year! Once they're gone, they're gone!" The advert ends with smiling customers carrying huge cardboard boxes to their cars.

This online advert for Trendy's new "Conscious Collection" shows models in soft beige and green clothes walking through a sunny field of tall wild flowers. Leaves and small birds appear in the corners of the screen. Calm, elegant text across the screen says, "Fashion that cares for the planet." The collection is presented on a special green page of the website, with a leaf symbol beside each item. However, the product labels show that most items contain only 1% recycled cotton. The rest of the website continues to sell hundreds of brand new styles every week at very low prices.

This TV advert for the Ridgeback SUV shows a large black car driving slowly down a busy, narrow city street. People on the pavement stop and turn to look at it. A group of young men nod in admiration, and a woman in a café smiles at the driver through the window. The driver, a man in his forties wearing dark sunglasses, parks in front of an expensive restaurant, and the doorman opens his door. The car never leaves the city, drives on rough ground or carries anything heavier than a shopping bag. The strapline appears: "Ridgeback. Make an entrance."

This online advert for the Spark dating app shows a series of short scenes of young people getting ready to go out: choosing clothes, practising a smile in the mirror, and taking a deep breath before entering a bar. Each person looks nervous and unsure at first, but calm and confident by the end of the scene. A voiceover says, "Be the person you want to be. Spark will help you find someone who loves them." Users' profile photos appear on screen, with descriptions such as "adventurous" and "creative". The advert ends with the line, "Your best self is waiting."

In a long corridor at a busy metro station, Fairway Bank has placed four posters in a row. The first shows only a large question: "Still paying bank fees?" The second shows a frustrated young woman looking at a bank charge on her phone. The third explains, in a few short lines, that Fairway's new account has no fees and pays interest every month. The fourth shows the same woman smiling, with the words, "Switch in ten minutes. Scan here." Each poster uses the same yellow background, and commuters see all four in order as they walk to the platform.

This TV advert for Edge's women's razors shows women of different ages, ethnicities and body shapes at the beach, at the gym and in the bathroom. Unlike most razor adverts, it shows real, natural body hair on legs, arms and underarms. Some women shave, while others choose not to, and neither choice is shown as better. A voiceover says, "Your body. Your choice. No judgement." There is no slow motion, no perfect lighting and no models with already smooth legs. The final screen shows the razor in simple pink and grey packaging, alongside the words, "Edge. For whatever you decide."

This TV advert for Homeguard insurance is filmed like a trailer for a superhero film. Loud, dramatic orchestral music builds, and a deep voice says, "In a world of burst pipes and broken windows, one hero stands ready." A man in an ordinary grey suit, holding a clipboard, walks in slow motion away from a small kitchen flood while sparks fly behind him. He arrives at a family's door and says, "Don't worry, I'm from Homeguard." The title appears in huge metal letters: "HOMEGUARD: THE CLAIM." The advert ends with the company's website and a phone number for making claims.

This online advert for the Pulse smartwatch shows a woman sleeping, running and working at a desk, while numbers and graphs float around her body. Her heart rate, sleep score, steps and stress level are all displayed in bright blue. Each number changes constantly, even while she is asleep or eating breakfast. At one point, a message appears on the watch: "Your recovery score is low. Rest today." The strapline appears in clean white letters: "Your body, measured." At the end, the advert says the watch comes with a free month of Pulse Premium, which then costs £8 a month.

This online advert for the Jet 200 printer shows the small white machine on a tidy desk beside a laptop and a small green plant. Large blue letters announce, "Only £30!" Below, three smiling students happily print bright, colourful posters for a school science project. However, the product page explains in small print that the printer only works with official Jet ink cartridges, which cost £40 for a set. It also says that cartridges from other brands will be blocked by a chip inside the printer. At the bottom, the advert also offers an "ink subscription" for £6 a month.

This TV advert for a Chinese supermarket chain shows a young woman travelling home from a big city on the night before Chinese New Year. Through the train window, red lanterns glow in every village. When she arrives, her grandmother is making dumplings at the kitchen table, and a whole steamed fish is being prepared for dinner. The room is filled with red decorations and paper cuttings of the character for "fortune". The family eat together as fireworks explode outside. The advert ends with the supermarket's logo and a short, gentle line in gold: "Home is where the table is."

In this online video, a popular fashion influencer sits on her bed surrounded by bright paper bags from Trendy. She takes out twenty items one by one, holding each one up to the camera and saying how cheap it was. "This top was only six pounds!" she says excitedly, laughing. Many of the items still have their price tags. She tries a few on and spins around happily in front of a mirror. In the caption, she lists every item with a link and a discount code. The video ends with her saying, "I'll be doing another haul next month!"

This online advert for SkyHop shows a plane flying through a clear blue sky above a thick green forest. The plane's tail is painted with a large green leaf. The headline says, "Fly carbon neutral with SkyHop." Below, smaller text explains that for an extra £3 per ticket, the airline will plant trees in Scotland to "balance" the carbon from each flight. A disclaimer at the bottom of the page says that the trees will take up to forty years to absorb the carbon. The advert gives no information about how much fuel the planes actually burn on each journey.

In the mobile game Kingdom Clash, a pop-up advert appears while players are in the middle of a battle. It shows a glowing golden chest that shakes, sparkles and flashes with coloured light, while exciting music plays. Text says, "Legendary skins: only available for 24 hours!" A countdown timer runs beside the chest. Players cannot see what is inside until they buy it with gems, which cost real money. A small line says the chance of finding a legendary item is two per cent. The game is rated suitable for players aged twelve and over, and most players are teenagers.

This online advert for Bean There coffee is made in the style of a 1920s silent film. It is in black and white, the picture is slightly shaky, and a piano plays quick, comic music. A tired man in a black bowler hat falls asleep at his desk, then wakes up and runs through the city, dodging cars and policemen, until he reaches a Bean There café. Old-fashioned title cards appear between scenes, such as "Mr Jones needed his coffee." When he finally takes his first sip, the whole screen bursts into full colour, and modern music begins to play.

This TV advert for the Volta car shows the car driving alone along a long, empty road through wide, green mountain valleys. There are no other vehicles, no buildings and no traffic lights. The sky is huge and blue, and the road disappears into the distance. The driver opens the window and puts her hand out into the wind. For a moment, a large eagle flies beside the car, level with the window. The only sound is quiet music and the wind. The final shot shows the car on a cliff edge at sunset, with the words, "Volta. Go further."

This Christmas advert for Hollins supermarket shows a mother preparing the family's Christmas dinner from early morning. She peels potatoes, stuffs the turkey and makes the sauce while her husband and children play noisy board games and watch television in the next room. When the meal is ready, everyone sits down and applauds her loudly. She smiles proudly and says, "It's worth it to see their faces." Warm music plays throughout, and the kitchen is full of steam. The strapline appears at the end: "Hollins. Making Christmas magic, together." In the advert, the father carries the turkey to the table.

This poster by a charity that campaigns for factory workers' rights looks almost exactly like a luxury advert for Maison Noir handbags. It uses the same plain white background, the same elegant gold font and the same type of large, glossy photograph. However, instead of a model, the person holding the handbag is a tired young woman in a factory, surrounded by rows of sewing machines. The slogan has been changed from "Only 100 made" to "Made by hands you'll never see." At the bottom, a line says that the worker earned less than the cost of the bag's zip.

This social media advert for Bliss bath bombs shows a young woman sinking into a bath full of pink and purple bubbles. Candles are burning around the bath, and her phone is switched off on a towel. Soft piano music plays, and she closes her eyes. The caption says, "You deserve this. Self-care starts at £6." Below, a voiceover says, "Because looking after yourself isn't selfish." The advert offers a box of twelve bath bombs as a "self-care subscription" that arrives every month. It appears mainly on Sunday evenings, when many young people are feeling stressed about the week ahead.

This streaming service has a homepage that automatically begins playing a trailer as soon as the user arrives. When an episode ends, the next one starts after just five seconds, with a countdown in the corner of the screen. The service describes itself as "endless stories for every mood". Cancelling the subscription requires the user to find a small link at the bottom of the account settings page, then answer three questions and click through two screens that ask, "Are you sure you want to miss out?" The free trial ends automatically after seven days, and payment begins without warning.

This billboard for Glacier water shows a plastic bottle standing on a large block of blue ice in front of snowy mountains. The bottle is clear and covered in cold drops of water, and the label is pale blue with a drawing of a mountain peak. The slogan says, "Pure as nature." In smaller letters, the billboard says, "Sourced from the Alps." There is no mention of the plastic bottle itself, what happens to it afterwards, or how far it travels to reach the shops. The billboard stands beside a motorway in a city two thousand kilometres from the Alps.

This TV advert for Volley sportswear follows a group of women in their seventies training for a marathon. They run together through a city park on cold, dark mornings, stretch on park benches and laugh about their sore knees and backs. One woman is seen collecting her granddaughter from school, still in her running clothes, with a medal around her neck. On race day, they cross the finish line together, holding hands. There are no young models in the advert. The final screen shows the women's ages, from 71 to 79, followed by the strapline, "Volley. Start whenever you want."

This poster for Kite phones shows an old, scratched phone lying in a museum display case, as if it were an ancient object. A small label beside it reads, "Kite 5, 2023." The lighting is dim, and the glass is slightly dusty. Next to the case, there is a photograph of the shiny, slim new Kite 8. The strapline says, "Your old phone is history." Below, smaller text offers up to £200 off when customers trade in their old phone. The poster appears in train stations and shopping centres across the country, two years after the Kite 5 was released.

This magazine advert for Maison Noir shows a young woman walking out of a famous luxury hotel in Paris, carrying a handbag covered in the brand's own logo: a repeated pattern of two gold letters, M and N. Her clothes are simple and black, so the bag is the only thing with a pattern. On the street, a photographer is taking her picture, and two other women turn to look at the bag as she passes. The only text is the brand's name in thin gold letters. The bag costs £2,800, but the price is not shown in the advert.

Every time a user opens the Bargain Hunt shopping app, a colourful prize wheel appears before they can see anything else. The wheel spins with flashing lights and cheerful sounds, and it always stops on a discount, such as 30% off, which is only valid for the next fifteen minutes. A countdown starts immediately. To close the wheel, the user must tap a tiny grey cross in the corner. Many of the discounts only apply if the user spends more than £40. Push notifications are sent to the user every evening, reminding users that their prizes are about to expire.

This fifteen-second TV advert for Surge energy drink begins with a close-up of a student yawning at a library desk covered in books, notes and empty coffee cups. A deep voice says, "Exam season?" She opens a can of Surge, and electric blue lightning bolts suddenly appear around her head, while dramatic music starts. In seconds, she is typing at lightning speed, answering exam questions, and then running out of the exam hall with her arms in the air. The voice says, "Surge. Unleash your inner genius." The final frame shows the blue can and the words, "Grab yours today."

This poster for Tasty Burger shows a famous Renaissance portrait of a woman with a mysterious smile. The painting looks exactly like the original, with the same dark background, soft light and folded hands. However, instead of resting her hands, she is now holding a large Tasty Burger, and a small amount of ketchup is on the side of her mouth. The caption says, "Now we know why she's smiling." The brand's logo appears once, in the corner, in the same gold as the old painting's frame. The poster is displayed in metro stations near the city's main art gallery.

This Christmas TV advert for a department store shows a family waking up on Christmas morning. The children run downstairs to find a huge, perfectly decorated tree surrounded by piles of beautifully wrapped presents. They open new phones, bikes, games consoles and designer clothes. Snow falls outside the window of their large, warm living room. Everyone is laughing and hugging, and nobody is shown without a gift. A voiceover says, "Give them the Christmas they deserve." The advert then shows a list of prices for each gift and offers a payment plan to "spread the cost into the new year".

This online advert for the NowNews app shows a young man standing on a crowded metro carriage. While everyone around him looks bored or tired, his phone buzzes with a notification: "Breaking: election results in." He reads it quickly, smiles and puts his phone back in his pocket. Later, at work, his colleagues in the office are amazed that he already knows the news. The strapline appears on screen: "NowNews. Know first." The advert ends by explaining that the app sends alerts within seconds of a story breaking, and that users can choose topics such as sport, business and technology.

This poster for Bolt e-scooters shows a scooter parked on a city street that has been covered in green leaves and grass, like a forest. Bright flowers grow around the wheels, and butterflies and small birds fly above it in the sunshine. The headline says, "Zero emissions. Zero guilt." The colour palette is almost entirely green. Small white text at the very bottom says that the scooters produce no exhaust fumes. However, the poster does not mention the batteries, the diesel vans that collect and charge the scooters every night, or how long each scooter lasts before it is replaced.

On the busiest shopping day of the year, a group of about fifty ordinary-looking people enter a large, crowded shopping centre at midday. Suddenly, at exactly the same moment, they all freeze in place: some holding empty shopping bags, others with their hands reaching towards shop windows. They stay completely still for five minutes while shoppers stare and film them on their phones. Then they unfold banners that read, "Buy Nothing Day: what do you really need?" and walk out together in silence. Videos of the event are shared widely online, and several news websites report on it that evening.

This online advert for the FitTrack fitness app shows a young woman running on a treadmill late at night, looking exhausted. On her phone screen, a picture of a pizza slowly appears as the calories she burns increase. When she reaches 800 calories, the pizza is complete, and a message says, "Well done! You've earned your dinner." The strapline appears: "FitTrack. Earn it." Every person who appears in the advert, including the people in the background of the gym, is very slim and toned. The advert ends with an offer of a free seven-day trial and then £9.99 a month.

This social media post by an expensive restaurant in Shanghai shows a dish of tiny, colourful vegetables arranged like a painting on a large black plate. Small pieces of gold leaf have been placed on top, and a single flower lies at the edge of the plate. The photo is taken from directly above, with perfect lighting. A diner's hand holds a phone over the plate, ready to take a photograph. The caption says, "Made to be shared." The restaurant tags every customer who posts a photo of their meal and gives them a free dessert on their next visit.

This magazine advert for Purity water shows a tall, heavy glass bottle with a silver cap on a white marble table. Next to it, a single crystal glass is filled with water and a thin slice of lemon. The label describes the water as "carefully filtered and mineral-balanced for the modern palate". The bottle costs £8 in restaurants, where it is served by waiters in white gloves. In very small print at the bottom of the page, the advert admits that the water comes from the city's ordinary public water supply, which is then filtered and bottled in a factory.

This online advert for the Fairway Bank app looks like a video game from the 1980s. The graphics are made of large pixels, and a cheerful, simple electronic tune plays in the background. A small pixel character jumps over obstacles labelled "fees", "debt" and "paperwork", collecting gold coins as he runs. When he reaches the end of the level, the words "Savings unlocked!" flash on the screen. The final screen changes to a modern photograph of a smiling woman in her late thirties using the app on her phone. The music stops, and the advert ends with the bank's logo.
